answer: A place I absolutely loved visiting as a child was my grandparents' village home, not far from Sirajganj, where they still live today. Although it is not a long journey, as a small boy it felt like travelling to another world. I went there with my parents and my two sisters, usually during the school holidays and always for Eid, and those visits are among my happiest childhood memories. Often my cousins came too, so the house would be full of noise and laughter. The house was surrounded by open fields and ponds, which felt like a [[boundless]] playground to a small child. I would spend whole days climbing mango trees, fishing with my grandfather and running around barefoot with my cousins. In the monsoon we would jump into the pond from the bank, and my grandmother would scold us and then feed us hot rice and fish. Everything felt wonderfully [[carefree]], far from the rules and routines of school and town life. What made it so special was the sense of freedom and the warmth of the whole extended family gathered together. The pace of life there was so gentle and [[unhurried]]. Honestly, looking back, those visits filled me with a deep sense of [[belonging]] that I still treasure. We still visit often, and my mother helps look after my grandparents, but the village has changed a lot since then, with more concrete houses and fewer open fields. Even so, the memories remain [[vivid]] and precious to me.

followUps.q: Do children today still enjoy visiting villages?
followUps.answer: Some do, but many are so used to screens that they get bored without the internet. My nephew loves it, though, especially chasing the chickens, so I think it depends on how children are introduced to it.

followUps.q: Do you still enjoy going there now?
followUps.answer: Very much, though for different reasons. Now I enjoy sitting with my grandparents, listening to their stories and helping them out, rather than climbing trees. It feels calm and grounding compared with work.

note: Grandparents still live in the village near Sirajganj; 'city life' changed to school and town life; added who went (parents, two sisters, cousins) and monsoon memories; plain 'endless' mark replaced by 'boundless', added 'vivid'.
